As a testament to the breadth of research areas that were involved from the beginning, the initial TalkBank grant proposal included a list of 50 researchers from 16 fields. Because of this wide range of disciplines, a critical feature of TalkBank was the creation of an inclusive transcription standard, called CHAT, that recognizes all the features required by these different disciplines for analyses. Now, the TalkBank system is the world's largest open access integrated repository for spoken language data. It has supported the process of understanding and modelling core issues such as how language is learned, how it is processed, how it changes, and how it can be restored after neurological damage (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?hrVZIU.

DARCLE consortium

Alongside the vision of Brian MacWhinney and the rapid uptake of the LENA system, the DARCLE community was formed with the goal of advancing relevant tools, resources, and knowledge. DARCLE, which stands for Daylong Audio Recordings of Children's Linguistic Environments, is a consortium of scholars and researchers around the world interested in naturalistic audio recordings, child and family speech, language development, computational analysis of spoken language, and related topics (http://www.darcle.org/). This group first started meeting in 2014, and initial discussions focused around standardizing consent processes, data sharing, security and ethics considerations for daylong audio, and building consistent processes for common and shared datasets. The main goals identified at these initial meetings were broadly to create 1) databanking infrastructure and 2) classification tools. Through collaboration with Brian MacWhinney and thanks to generous support of the National Science Foundation (via a RIDIR grant), this group of researchers helped establish a new component of TalkBank: HomeBank (VanDam et al., 2016). HomeBank is a repository founded in 2016 of raw longform recordings, some with transcriptions or diarized output, collected in the home and other naturalistic environments (e.g. childcare settings). Corpora also include demographic, family, and personal data relevant to the recordings and the interlocutors or environments. Another goal of HomeBank was to create an open code repository, where researchers could share code that they have created to process and analyze longform recordings. Shared code includes, for example, the rlena R Package, which can help researchers process LENA files (i.e. interpreted time segment files, https://github.com/HomeBankCode/rlena), and ChildProject, which is intended to standardize specifications and tools for the storage and management of longform recordings (Gautheron et al., 2023).

One frequent topic of discussion at DARCLE's early meetings was what kind of information individual research groups were attending to during transcriptions. While CHAT provides information and a robust system for transcribing speech, it is often agnostic (or not specific) about segmentation and timing, and about the addressee (i.e., to whom speech is directed, which is useful, for instance, in quantifying childdirected vs. adult-directed speech). As this type of data became more common, new processes were also needed to maximize the information that could be gleaned from these recordings. DARCLE members realized that it was worth thinking towards automated tools that could increasingly be leveraged on 'big' longform data, with the vision of integrating manual annotations with the burgeoning set of automated tools that had started to explode from speech engineers and computer scientists. With the goal of integrating across datasets and building automated tools, a subset of DARCLE members were able to obtain funding for a project entitled Analyzing Child Language Experiences around the World (ACLEW), which was funded via a unique TransAtlantic Platform Mechanism. Researchers in the ACLEW project agreed on a set of tiers (e.g. speakers, addressee, vocal maturity) that would be used to capture children's input and production. Generalizing from these transcription approaches, Casillas et al., (2017) proposed a standardized annotation system, now called the DARCLE Annotation Scheme (DAS), which provides a pipeline for a flexible and systematic annotation scheme that shares consistent features across labs while also allowing individual labs to add details as needed. Critically, exemplary of ACLEW's and DARCLE's commitment to open science and reproducibility, the ACLEW annotation scheme is accompanied by training modules and gold standard tests (for Windows and Mac, in English and Spanish) that can be used to train new researchers and research assistants on the annotation scheme before transcribing new recordings (see the associated https://osf.io/b2jep/wiki?wiki=b4he2). The experience creating materials and annotating the corpora brought together by the ACLEW project was described https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?TYtOkT.

Alongside the development of a shared annotation system, DARCLE members were also interested in understanding commonalities and differences in language input across corpora. For example, there was an interest in understanding to whom speech was directed during longform recordings. DARCLE researchers pooled resources to create a dataset of speech clips from daylong recordings that had been tagged as either containing adult-directed speech or child-directed speech. Findings from this dataset reveal that North American infants hear 2-3 times as much child-directed speech from female adult caregivers as from male adult caregivers, and that the proportion of child-directed speech increases as children get older (Bergelson, Casillas, et al., 2019). While the findings from this study are important in and of themselves, this was also one of the first papers (to our knowledge) to combine daylong recordings from different corpora to answer questions that would not have been possible with recordings from a single project or lab. This approach of combining longform recordings from different sources to answer larger-scale questions about language development has since continuedhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jF8XPj for examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?25g4tD with studies (also including DARCLE membershttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?csvZO8 measuring how the burstiness of speech is related to language development (Cychosz et al., 2025) , investigating how financial concerns may systematically affect child-directed speech (Ellwood-Lowe et al., 2022) , and examining cross-linguistic differences in language input (Bunce et al., 2025 ).

As a last example, we want to highlight not just the research findings and the tools that DARCLE members have supported, but also the incredible attention to detail that the DARCLE community has given to making science and longform recordings an ethical tool for data collection that allows us to also diversify science. In brief, the increased popularity of longform recordings, coupled with the relative ease and unintrusiveness of collecting this type of data, led to novel challenges. For example, because these methods allow for recordings of real-life experiences, they risk capturing and revealing experiences that individuals or groups would not have planned to share. To that endhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?BXu109 DARCLE members have written an article on best practices for the use of longform recordings (Cychosz et al., 2020) , which provides a set of ethical guidelines, alongside templates for consent documents and FAQs for participants.

Beyond considering how to ethically broaden the communities from which this data can be collectedhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cx1Eym DARCLE members have also published step-by-step guides for collecting and analyzing longform recordings (Casillas & Cristia, 2019; Pisani et al., 2021) , and organized and led workshops for researchers interested in learning more about this methodology, including The Workshop on Extensive and Intensive Recordings of Children's Language Environments (https://web.archive.org/web/20260714141731/https:/www.risc.cnrs.fr/manifestation/152345) in 2015, and the https://web.archive.org/web/20260714142021/https:/lfris2025.sciencesconf.org/?forward-action=index&forward-controller=index&lang=en in 2025. These are invaluable resources for researchers around the world who are considering using this methodology for the first time or with a new population, and want to make sure they consider all possible ethical concerns related to data collection, analysis, and sharing.

Nods to other collaborative communities

We would be remiss to not mention that DARCLE exists within a broader network of collaborative initiatives in developmental science. The Consortium on Language Variation in Input Environments around the World (LangView; https://alecristia.github.io/LangVIEW/), for example, is a collaborative network focused on understanding how children's language experiences across diverse environments shape language development, with a particular emphasis on the causal links between input and outcomes. LangView has close ties to DARCLE, reflected in the significant overlap in their goals and memberships. The Learning Variability Network Exchange (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?xIsIOG Frank et al., 2025) is a network of researchers focused on understanding relationships between variation in children's early experiences and developmental outcomes while also advancing collaborative and open science. Other collaborative initiatives include ManyBabies (Frank et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?pUUIR0 2017; ManyBabies Consortium et al., 2020) , which conducts large-scale collaborative studies in infancy research and the Acquisition Sketch Project (https://acquisition-sketch.phil-fak.uni-koeln.de/), an initiative aiming to expand knowledge on understudied languages. Together, these communities highlight the growing emphasis on collaboration in developmental science, with DARCLE uniquely contributing a focus on longform recording methodologies.

Building research in community

While the initial DARCLE meetings focused on sharing challenges and developing solutions to those challenges, meetings have since shifted to also include paper discussions and project presentations. These meetings, and the community more generally, have resulted in co-authored manuscripts, jointly developed resources for the field, collaborative grants, valuable feedback on ongoing work, and exposure to and development of impactful new technologies. We believe that this community embodies the importance of scientific collaborative consortia.

In part, these benefits have been possible because of our deliberate effort to maximize the inclusivity of DARCLE across career stages, communities, universities, and research areas. We prioritize having a very low barrier to group entry-anyone can join the listserv if they are interested and receive announcements about upcoming meetings and calls for participation. Since 2015, DARCLE has also had a New Investigators group, a subgroup of early career researchers (e.g., graduate students, postdocs) that meets monthly to discuss papers, research challenges, and provides additional focused support, including, for example, sessions about navigating the academic job market (e.g., finding opportunities, applying for jobs, interviewing). Importantly, New Investigator members are encouraged to attend both types of meetings; our goal is not to impose a hierarchy but to provide an additional space to meet scholars at similar career stages to build connections.

At the same time, DARCLE leaders continually face challenges that arise from organizing a group of researchers from around the world. For example, like many research collaboratives, our community spans multiple time zones (e.g., Pacific Time, Central European Time, India Standard Time, and Japan Standard Time), which can make attendance challenging for all members. To address this, we have purposely varied the time of our meetings such that they are more (or less) convenient for all members throughout the year, and aim not to prioritize one time zone over others. An additional way to bridge this challenge has been for researchers around the world to also form "sister groups" that meet more frequently at a convenient time for them, such as the recently established DARCLE Asia (https://darcle-asia.org/). We have learned that to be maximally inclusive also means to inconvenience some members, and board members pay special attention to not always inconveniencing the same people. While subgroups of DARCLE have had success securing funding for specific projects (i.e. Homebank, ACLEW), securing funding for resources like website hosting and maintenance and other day-to-day operations has been a challenge, as most funding sources do not have mechanisms for funding collaborative initiatives. Despite these challenges, the rewards of leading and engaging in groups like DARCLE are substantial, with past and present members working together to sustain its progress.

As we continue to grow DARCLE and conduct research to learn more about language development through naturalistic longform recordings, we are excited about the advances we see on the horizon. While longform recordings have allowed researchers to make significant progress in terms of the contexts in which children's language development is studied (Rowe & Weislederhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?UB4grM 2020) , there are still many environments that are under-represented. Our systematic search of the literature found that longform recording papers span 58 languages (see Supplementals). At the same time, a recent meta-analysis showed that the vast majority of published studies examining the relationship between language input and outcomes have been conducted in the United States or other English-speaking countries (Coffey & Snedeker, 2026).

Nonetheless, researchers have been using these technologies in a number of ways to capture more diverse contexts. For example, technological advances such as wearable, low-cost USB recorders have allowed researchers to expand data collection to remote or understudied populations, and to conduct larger-scale studies (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Db92gn Coffey et al., 2026). To complement audio recordingshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LAtX9V researchers have also begun incorporating ecological momentary assessment (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LAtX9V Nencheva et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?43fBDp 2026) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gDvSBa movement and body position sensors (Rousey et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?4MsBMe 2026) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Hav0Ig photo capture (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gDvSBa Casillas et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?02mgou 2020) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?diMzK3 head-mounted cameras (Long et al., 2023; Sullivan et al., 2021) , eye-tracking (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Hav0Ig Ståhlberg-Forsén et al., 2023) , EEG (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?02mgou Marklund et al., 2019) , and electrocardiogram (ECG) measurements (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?diMzK3 Wass et al., 2021 Wass et al., , 2022 Wass et al., , 2024 Wass et al., , 2025)) , among other methods. Integrating these methods with longform recordings can provide supplemental information sources that can be integrated into coding schemes (e.g., for speaker identification and audio context characterization) and/or characterize the varying contexts in which everyday input occurs around the world.

As we continue to diversify and increase our populations of study, we also need continued technological advancements that will help us process and analyse this data. The cornerstone technology and software used for longform recordings (LENA) has been trained exclusively on data from North American, English-speaking families with children between 1 and 48 months in their homes (Gilkerson et al., 2008 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7EdWTN Gilkerson et al., 2017). Thus, LENA's reported accuracy cannot be assumed to automatically generalize to other populations, languages, ages, or environments (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?X5iWsQ Cristia et al., 2020 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?X5iWsQ https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?RBAfbY Bastianello et al., 2024; Coffey & Cristia, 2024; Egan-Dailey & Bergelson, 2026; Lavechin et al., 2020; Meera et al., 2025; Räsänen et al., 2021). Recently, open-source alternatives to the LENA software have been developed. Here too, members of the DARCLE community have pioneered these, or provided the open-source data to make these developments possible. For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ZLNnKL Voice-Type Classifier (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ZLNnKL Lavechin et al., 2020) , a tool directly developed thanks to the ACLEW data and funding, is an open-source speaker diarization software that was trained on recordings from multiple languages and across more diverse settings (i.e., rural and urban). Furthermore, VTC can accommodate overlapping speech (Lavechin et al., 2020; ), which may render it more suitable for studying diverse language environments, including bilingual and multilingual communities (Cristia et al., 2023) and/or indigenous and under-researched language communities (Coffey et al., 2026). ACLEW also allowed the development of ALICEhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Q4iNax an Automatic Linguistic Unit Count Estimator (Räsänen et al., 2021) , which estimates the number of adultspoken linguistic units in an open source alternative to LENA's Adult Word Count estimates. Importantly, ALICE was designed as a language-neutral measure for diverse linguistic contexts, and was trained on Argentinian Spanish, Tseltal, Yeli Dnye, and American and UK variants of English.

More recentlyhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?JKuieo efforts to go beyond the original VTC has resulted in integrated tools like WSW2 (Sun et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?nnlY6f 2025) , which combines a voice type classifier with the Whisper Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model to generate transcriptions of both adult and child speech; and HARMONI (Weng et al., 2025) , which further incorporates video signals. Also of note is BabyHUBERT (Charlot et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?HyrUI8 2026) , a self-supervised (i.e. pre-trained) speech representation model trained on multilingual (40+ languages) infant-centered data, which can serve as an ideal basis on top of which to create special purpose classifiers, such as BabAR, see below.

Moving forward, we look forward to advances that allow us to transcribe child speech from longform recordings as a way to more precisely capture linguistic features of child talk. Recent research has explored using Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to transcribe speech from children, but a challenge in this work is that the Large Language Models that were used to develop the most comprehensive ASR softwares (e.g., WhisperX) were trained primarily on adult speech. Work is currently underway to explore the precision of these ASR programs (Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025; Tang et al., 2025) and create new pipelines that can produce usable metrics from these imperfect transcripts. Building on the Voice Type Classifiers discussed above, Lavechin et al. (2026) have recently developed BabAR (Babbling Automatic Recognition), an end-to-end algorithm for transcribing children's utterances into the phonemes they produce. BabAR was trained on Englishhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7H5P4j French, Portuguese, German, and Spanish data from CHILDES and Phonbank (a Talkbank subset, Rose & Stoel-Gammon, 2015) , and then evaluated on the SEEDLingS corpus (on Homebank, Bergelson, 2017), further highlighting the ways in which these data repositories and open science practices continue to make scientific advances possible.

As technological advances continue to improve, we are excited to see more work on communities and speakers that have historically been excluded. For example, existing algorithms cannot automatically distinguish which language(s) are being used, so researchers studying bilingual contexts have had to rely on manual annotations of the language(s) children hear and use in longform recordings (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?IE9N9W Orena et al., 2020). Work is underway to explore the use of new ASR technology to automatically transcribe and detect which languages are being spoken in shorter recordings (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wueW4F Wu et al., 2025) and we look forward to research extending these pipelines to daylong recordings. Similarly, most prior research has focused on measuring linguistic units from adult speech, and ignored speech from other children altogether. With advances such as BabAR, we are excited to see research move forward with also capturing speech from other children, which is a common feature of children's experiences around the world that has largely been ignored in our theories of language development (Bulgarelli, 2026). We look forward to more technological advances that continue to make diversifying the samples we study more feasible for a range of researchers who may or may not have the resources to manually annotate and transcribe this type of data.

Closing remarks

In order to further strengthen the contribution of research using longform recordings, we close with a series of recommendations.

 Our systematic search of the literature revealed wide-ranging keywords, which made it difficult to identify all the uses of this methodology to date. We recommend that going forward, authors use a more consistent set of keywords referring to longform recordings, so that the scope of the literature can be fully evident. Authors may consider using "daylong recordings", "longform recordings", "LENA recordings" and/or "LENA system". Of note, we recommend against using "LENA" as a keyword on its own, as this keyword is also used to describe the Lena River Delta, which is the largest in the world (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?8kYty4)  We also encourage authors to more thoroughly describe their participant populations, listing both the country in which the participants were sampled and the language(s) in use. We noticed that many papers (~25-30%) currently omit some or all of this information, particularly if the data was collected in North America and/or with English speaking communities (see Supplementals). This pattern leads to centering the North American English speaking context, which may distract from the goal of identifying both universal similarities and cultural differences in the process of child language learning (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?iR2OiB Scaff et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2024 Singh et al., , 2025) )  To continue building resources, we also recommend that researchers continue to share their recordings and/or annotations on platforms that make them available to other researchers (i.e. Homebank for longform recordings, CHILDES and Databrary for other shorter recordings), and to openly share their code.  We encourage researchers interested in topics related to language input and longform recordings to join the DARCLE community. We further suggest that other researchers create their communities of like-minded scholars. At a time when science is under threat, working together to advance our shared goals is the best way forward.

We believe that to continue to make progress on our shared goal of understanding how children's experiences relate to their language development, we will need to continue relying on scientific communities like DARCLE (and those that DARCLE is built on). The current empirical challenges are solvable with creative collaborations between researchers across disciplines and with continued sharing of data (in raw form and with partial or full annotations) that can be used for training new algorithms and answering new questions. We look forward to seeing the ways in which these communities and methodologies continue to advance our understanding of the relationship between children's language input and their language development. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, ERIC, CINAHL, DBLP, OpenAIRE, and Arxiv were searched. A search strategy was developed using keywords including variations of 'daylong recordings', 'longform recordings', 'LENA System', 'LENA recordings,' and 'automated vocal analysis.' The search was completed in February 2026 and had no date restrictions. Covidence Software (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?y9K8y8) was used to organize the studies for further analysis. Following this first round of extraction, two rounds of post-hoc search were conducted based on updated keywords to ensure inclusion of papers the authors identified as missing from the initial search. These additional keywords were: 'all day recordings,' 'naturalistic recordings,' 'language environment data,' and 'wearable microphone'. Additionally, post-hoc, six papers were added manually by authors. One of the manually added studies was identified as not using longform audio data (see below) and ultimately, was excluded. The post-hoc searches were completed in April 2026 and had no date restrictions. See https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode/blob/main/Data/A0_MetadataFiles/SF2_ManualAddition_DARCLESuggestions.xlsx (SF2) for a list of papers identified as not included by authors, resulting in the updated keyword post-hoc searches. See https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode/blob/main/Data/A0_MetadataFiles/SF1a_CovidenceFinalExport_2026_05.csv (SF1a) for the summary spreadsheet exported from Covidence.

After removing duplicates, two authors completed title/abstract screening and full text review (HG, VPSR). Studies were included if they reported the use of longform recordings to investigate children's language acquisition and vocal development. Conference abstracts, dissertations, and papers not written in English were excluded (see Fig. S1 for details). Some duplicate entries and studies not written in English were only identified after data extraction (see below, as well as Fig. S1). A version of the summary spreadsheet exported from Covidence with rows corresponding to these duplicate entries removed-and which was used for post-extraction data analyses-is available as https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode/blob/main/Data/A0_MetadataFiles/SF1_CovidenceFinalExport_2026_05_DupesRem.xlsx (SF1).

which no categories could be automatically extracted (with the exception of research projects and community). Complete results of data extraction and full citations can be found in the associated https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode.

Limitations

This search was completed to illustrate the breadth of existing research engaging longform audio recordings to investigate child language environments. Efficiency was valued over rigor, which led to significant limitations. Some eligible studies may have been missed in our search. In fact, six papers were added manually by the authors because they were not identified via our search terms. Many papers used the keyword 'LENA'. Including 'LENA' as a search term results in tens of thousands of returns from databases, as this keyword also describes the Lena River Delta, thereby making it infeasible as a search term to identify studies that use longform recordings (see also Closing Remarks in the main text). Abstract screening and full text review were conducted by one reviewer per paper. Thus, while multiple reviewers contributed to abstract screening and full text review, there was no redundancy provided by more than one reviewer screening an abstract or reviewing the full text of a study, which may have led to mistaken inclusions or exclusions. Similarly, manual extraction and review was completed by one reviewer per paper, potentially leading to incorrect results. Automated extraction relied on keywords without additional context. As a result, the automated extraction may misrepresent results in some cases, and papers that used terms that did not match our keywords might be incorrectly extracted. Notably, extraction for topics and communities/consortia did not undergo further manual review for extraction and are, therefore, at high risk for misrepresentation (see associated https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode for details). Additionally, we excluded papers not in English, limiting our results. By providing the full citations and results as well as access to the data extraction code, we invite those interested to more rigorously investigate the literature while cautiously interpreting our findings.

Search strategy and data extraction

A systematic search of the literature was conducted to identify scientific literature using daylong audio recordings to investigate child language environments.

Data extraction included:

 Citation, including paper title, author list, year of publication, and journal/ venue of publication. These details were derived from the summary spreadsheet exported from Covidence. As such, some entries may have missing information (see Supplementary Files https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode/blob/main/Data/A0_MetadataFiles/SF1_CovidenceFinalExport_2026_05_DupesRem.xlsx and https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode/blob/main/Data/A0_MetadataFiles/SF1a_CovidenceFinalExport_2026_05.csv (SF1 and SF1a) for details).  Type of study (observational, experimental, best practices, commentaries, computational, validation, review, other-e.g., feasibility or sampling), as designated by one of the authors (HG; see below). For the type of study, two additional types were added at the manual review and extraction (see below) stage-non-longform and non-English content-to identify studies that were included in the extracted database that respectively, did not use longform audio data or were written in a language other than English (see https://github.com/Ritwikavps/DARCLEPaper2025_ExtractionCode/blob/main/Data/A0_MetadataFiles/SF3_DARCLE_ExtractionList_Unified.xlsx (SF3)). Figure 1.

Figure 1. Number of publications (including peer-reviewed journal articles, pre-prints, conference papers, and books) included in our high-level systematic search as a function of published year and publication type (see legend). There are three distinct phases in the timeline of using longform recordings to study children's language development: a 'sparse' phase (1979-1985) and a 'dense' phase (2009 onwards, coinciding with the release of LENA). These two phases are separated by an 'inactive' period (1986-2009; indicated in grey), and these three phases have different x-axis scales to aid visualization. The release of LENA (2009) and the formation of DARCLE (2014) are also indicated. The number of publications as a function of publication year is provided with a uniform temporal scale in the inset.

All extracted categories and associated details were determined through discussion between authors based on experience and expertise using daylong recordings. Extraction was completed using a combination of automated and manual strategies. After full text review, one author reviewed all included papers and designated 'type' (HG). Further extraction was not completed for papers assigned best practices, com- mentaries, computational, validation, review, or other. One author (VPSR) created a custom algorithm to automatically extract recording device, software, manual an- notation, country, language, topic, and community/consortia details from the obser- vational and experimental papers. Details of the automated extraction process can be found in the associated GitHub repository. Not all studies could be automatically ex- tracted. Additionally, some studies required manual review for some categories. Manual review and extraction for these studies were done by four authors (AP, VPSR, AM, HG). At the manual review and extraction stage, some studies were re-typed (e.g., from experimental/observational to review; see Supplementary Files 3a and 3b (SF3a and SF3b) for details). Further, some duplicates were identified after the manual re- view and extraction stage via a custom algorithm (see Fig S1).

papers were included in the final analysis (see Figure S1 for PRISMA flowchart), including 242 (64.02%) observational and experimental studies. For some of the pa- pers, not all information could be automatically extracted, and thus manual review and extraction was carried out. Specifically, we manually extracted recording device for 33 papers (13.63%), software for 58 papers (23.97%), country and language for 136 papers (56.2%), manual annotation for 20 papers (8.26%), and topic for 20 papers (8.26%).
